respuesta: Both treat the knowledge graph as an external, structural memory substrate that indexes associations rather than storing raw content. HippoRAG frames its LLM-extracted open KG as a hippocampal index: the neocortex (LLM) stores representations while the graph holds interconnected pointers and associations, enabling pattern separation at encoding and pattern completion at retrieval [2405.14831#s5.p1][2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s4.p1]. The agent-memory survey places knowledge graphs under external memory's "structural store" substrate, which scales and supports explicit editing but adds retrieval latency and depends on retrieval/ranking quality, with no substrate dominating so designs hybridize [2602.06052#s8.p1][2602.06052#s8.p2][2602.06052#s17.p6]. For the algorithm: HippoRAG extracts query named entities, links them to the most cosine-similar KG nodes, and runs Personalized PageRank over the KG with a personalized distribution uniform on those query nodes (damping factor 0.5), then multiplies the resulting node distribution by the passage-node count matrix to score passages; node specificity s_i=|P_i|^{-1} scales query-node probabilities before PPR [2405.14831#s6.p2][2405.14831#s6.p4][2405.14831#s6.p5][2405.14831#s11.p1].

HippoRAG 2 exposes knowledge as a graph index: an LLM extracts schemaless OpenIE triples whose subjects/objects are phrase nodes and edges are relation edges, plus synonym edges from embedding similarity and passage nodes linked by "contains" context edges, forming an open KG with sparse conceptual and dense contextual coding [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. Retrieval is a single graph-search step: the query is matched to triples, an LLM filter keeps relevant triples as seeds, and Personalized PageRank ranks passages [2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. HippoRAG 2 exposes knowledge as a graph index: offline, an LLM extracts schemaless OpenIE triples whose subjects/objects are phrase nodes and edges are relation edges, plus synonym edges between similar phrases and passage nodes linked by "contains" context edges, forming an open KG with sparse conceptual and dense contextual coding [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. Retrieval is a single-shot graph operation: the query matches triples, an LLM filter keeps relevant triples as seed nodes, and Personalized PageRank ranks passages [2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. Its structural artifact is thus the passage-integrated knowledge graph (phrase/relation/synonym/passage nodes) traversed by PPR.

LLM-Wiki instead exposes knowledge as a persistent, human-readable Wiki: directory indices, structured Markdown pages with metadata, aliases, tags, facts, source references, and bidirectional wikilinks, compiled incrementally against current Wiki state [2605.25480#s9.p1][2605.25480#s9.p2]. Retrieval is agent-planned compositional traversal via wiki_search and wiki_read, following links (direct access, bridge link-following, exploratory browsing) rather than a fixed graph algorithm [2605.25480#s11.p2][2605.25480#s12.p2]. Its structural artifact is the linked wiki page set (plus an Error Book for self-correction) [2605.25480#s8.p1][2605.25480#s15.p1]. In short: HippoRAG 2 = LLM-extracted KG + PPR; LLM-Wiki = compiled linked wiki pages + agent traversal.

respuesta: WikiLoop explicitly uses downstream feedback to improve its structured knowledge base: it couples Wiki construction to the downstream Navigator within one role-conditioned policy, since construction normally receives no signal from downstream use [2607.26604#s1.p1]. The Builder's reward is the marginal change in navigation utility ΔU, measured by running a frozen Navigator on the Wiki before and after each patch, with guard queries penalizing regressions [2607.26604#s7.p2][2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p14]; this feedback trains the Builder and jointly the Navigator via RL [2607.26604#s5.p7]. HippoRAG 2 does not use downstream feedback to improve its knowledge base: its graph is built offline by LLM OpenIE triple extraction plus synonym and passage/context edges [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2], and retrieval uses query-to-triple matching, an LLM triple filter, and Personalized PageRank [2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s10.p1][2502.14802#s11.p1]. The page describes no training or edit loop driven by downstream QA performance; the LLM is used online for filtering, not for learning from downstream utility. In short, WikiLoop treats downstream navigation utility as the training signal shaping its Wiki edits [2607.26604#s7.p14], whereas HippoRAG 2's structured index is constructed offline with no downstream-feedback optimization [2502.14802#s7.p4].

They differ in whether downstream feedback is used to train the knowledge base at all. WikiLoop explicitly couples construction to downstream use: it trains one role-conditioned policy whose Builder reward is the marginal downstream navigation utility of each edit, measured by running a frozen Navigator on the Wiki before and after the patch, with guard queries penalizing regressions [2607.26604#s7.p2][2607.26604#s7.p8][2607.26604#s7.p14]. HippoRAG 2, by contrast, builds its knowledge graph offline via LLM OpenIE triples plus synonym and passage nodes, and its online components (query-to-triple matching, LLM triple filtering, PPR) are used for retrieval only; the page describes no training of the index from downstream answer quality [2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2][2502.14802#s9.p1][2502.14802#s10.p1]. So WikiLoop learns the structured KB from downstream feedback, while HippoRAG 2 uses a fixed, heuristically constructed graph and applies LLM reasoning only at query time.

respuesta: The key difference is single-shot dense retrieval versus agent-controlled iterative lexical search. Raw-RAG is a one-pass pipeline: it embeds the question, retrieves the 128 nearest 256-token windows by cosine similarity, reranks with a cross-encoder, and passes the top 15 to the reader [2610.30755#s6.p3]; it is the degenerate case of one retrieval round with no reformulation [2608.12888#s18.p1]. ReFind instead runs a ReAct-style loop in which the LLM chooses keywords and parameters over multiple rounds (up to 4 iterations, K=5), using turn-granularity BM25 plus four chat-native controls: session-aware RRF fusion, ±2-turn context expansion, temporal filtering, and seen-session deduplication [2608.12888#s10.p1][2608.12888#s22.p1][2608.12888#s13.p5][2608.12888#s15.p1][2608.12888#s16.p1][2608.12888#s17.p1]. Thus ReFind defers the retrieval decision to query time through adaptive multi-round agent control over raw text, whereas Raw-RAG fixes a single dense-retrieval-plus-rerank pass [2608.12888#s9.p1][2610.30755#s6.p1].

pasos.argumento: ReFind Raw-RAG raw chat history retrieval

respuesta: Both retrieve from unmodified raw chat history without building semantic structure, but they differ in retrieval mechanism and control. Raw-RAG is single-shot dense retrieval: it embeds 256-token windows, retrieves the top 128 by cosine similarity, reranks with a cross-encoder, and passes the top 15 to the reader [2610.30755#s6.p2][2610.30755#s6.p3]. ReFind instead gives a ReAct agent iterative, controllable lexical (BM25) search at turn granularity, with four chat-native controls—RRF session fusion, ±2-turn context expansion, temporal filtering, and seen-session deduplication—over up to 4 rounds [2608.12888#s10.p1][2608.12888#s22.p1][2608.12888#s13.p5][2608.12888#s15.p1][2608.12888#s16.p1][2608.12888#s17.p1]. In short, Raw-RAG is a fixed one-shot dense retrieve-and-rerank pipeline, whereas ReFind is agent-controlled multi-round lexical search with query reformulation and chat-native filters [2608.12888#s18.p1].

respuesta: Agent Zero Memory treats knowledge updates as versioned, provenance-bearing assertions rather than overwrites: each assertion records origin, an immutable timestamp, and an evidence pointer, and its citation-locked reading discipline structurally excludes fabrication [2608.29606#s6.p2][2608.29606#s6.p3][2608.29606#s6.p4]. It criticizes systems that overwrite silently or accrete contradictions, and instead avoids epistemic loss by versioning updates rather than overwriting [2608.29606#s1.p2][2608.29606#s3.p7]. Its design principle is provenance with calibrated belief under a citation lock, plus layering of raw sources, curated facts, and inferred experience [2608.29606#s6.p5]. Raw-RAG takes the opposite stance: it indexes raw, unprocessed history with no LLM extraction, summarization, graph construction, or mutation, leaving resolution of temporal order and state changes to the reader [2610.30755#s6.p2][2610.30755#s6.p3]. It argues mutation is largely unnecessary: UPDATE and DELETE are only about 4.4% of LoCoMo and 2.5% of LongMemEval write decisions, and replacing UPDATE with ADD and DELETE with NONE raises LoCoMo accuracy from 67.36% to 69.42% [2610.30755#s2.p3][2610.30755#s2.p6]. Its design principle is that raw evidence coverage, not write-time curation, drives performance: Raw-RAG has the highest evidence coverage (45.29% on MemoryAgentBench, 76.35% on MEME) and highest conditional path coverage (62.34%), while adding atomic-fact extraction, summaries, or graph expansion lowers scores by 19.62, 5.81, and 5.78 points [2610.30755#s15.p7][2610.30755#s16.p3][2610.30755#s12.p1].

respuesta: Agent Zero Memory treats knowledge updates as versioned, provenance-bearing assertions rather than silent overwrites: it argues that when a user corrects a fact, systems should not overwrite silently or accrete contradictions, and it records each assertion with origin, immutable timestamp, and evidence pointer, with answers citation-locked to opened items [2608.29606#s1.p2][2608.29606#s6.p2][2608.29606#s6.p3]. Its design principle is a durable, queryable, honest model of what is known — provenance with calibrated belief under a citation lock, plus layering of raw sources, curated facts, and inferred experience [2608.29606#s1.p3][2608.29606#s6.p5]. Raw-RAG takes the opposite stance: it indexes raw history with no LLM extraction, summarization, graph construction, or mutation, and lets the reader resolve temporal order and state changes itself [2610.30755#s6.p2][2610.30755#s6.p3]. Its principle is that complex mutation is unnecessary — UPDATE/DELETE are only 4.39% of LoCoMo and 2.46% of LongMemEval write decisions, replacing UPDATE with ADD and DELETE with NONE raises LoCoMo accuracy from 67.36% to 69.42%, and raw evidence lets the reader handle cascades and invalidation [2610.30755#s2.p3][2610.30755#s2.p6][2610.30755#s2.p7]. So Agent Zero emphasizes provenance-preserving epistemic honesty, while Raw-RAG emphasizes preserving raw evidence and delegating state reconstruction to the reader.

The two papers reach opposite headline verdicts. The preregistered agent-browsed comparison (2605.18490) does not crown a winner: the compiled wiki only weakly supports the synthesis hypothesis (structural_integrity +1.625 judge-averaged, below the registered +2.0 threshold; inter_paper_mapping +6.625) [2605.18490#s26.p2], point-source groundedness parity is fragile (+0.667 judge-averaged, P(mu≥0)=0.660) [2605.18490#s27.p3], and on corrected claim-level scoring RAG's cited claims are supported 53.8% vs 41.5% for the wiki [2605.18490#s37.p6]; the wiki also costs ~21x more query tokens [2605.18490#s28.p2]. By contrast, the classroom comparison (2609.25303) finds the compiled wiki clearly ahead overall (9.95 vs 9.05 of 10; grounded 98% vs 81%) [2609.25303#s16.p2][2609.25303#s16.p3], and even on single-fact topic-page questions (9.96 vs 9.33) [2609.25303#s16.p5], with the advantage roughly tripling on cross-page questions (score gap 1.79 vs 0.62) [2609.25303#s16.p6].

The key factor they identify is the serving/context-selection strategy of the wiki arm: in 2605.18490 the wiki is browsed by a tool-using agent that pays for its own traversal (up to 30 turns) [2605.18490#s8.p1], whereas in 2609.25303 the wiki arm has no context-selection step that can fail, so the authors read their result as the gap between real retrieval and perfect context selection [2609.25303#s24.p3]. The concept page frames the disagreement as verdicts depending on serving strategy, baseline, scoring, and judge [2605.18490#s8.p1], noting that a decomposition-retrieval RAG variant closes ~94% of the synthesis gap at lower cost [2605.18490#s44.p2][2605.18490#s44.p4].

respuesta: WiCER's loop is reactive: it evaluates the compiled wiki with one diagnostic probe per source document, and any probe scoring 1/5 triggers diagnosis of the dropped facts, which are fed back as preservation constraints (pinning) in the next compilation — i.e., CEGAR where the document collection is the concrete system, the wiki the abstraction, a score-1 probe the counterexample, and pinning the refinement [2605.07068#s37.p1][2605.07068#s36.p1]. Streaming Knowledge Compilation (Online WiCER) removes the static-corpus assumption and replaces this reactive probe-driven pinning with proactive pinning driven by a predicted materiality signal φ̂_t, adding decay-weighted eviction and periodic full recompilation every T_r steps, with O(√(T log K)) regret plus a prediction-error term [2606.09877#s2.p3][2606.09877#s31.p2][2606.09877#s43.p3]. Queries cannot drive pinning because they arrive after the news batch, so a bounded materiality signal φ_t(k,n)∈[0,1] acts as a query-relevance surrogate and facts are pinned before any query exposes a gap [2606.09877#s19.p2][2606.09877#s2.p3]. The key conceptual shift is 'predictive CEGAR': the counterexample becomes a predicted high-materiality news item rather than an observed QA failure, moving refinement from diagnosis to prediction [2606.09877#s42.p1][2606.09877#s42.p4].

pasos.argumento: Streaming Knowledge Compilation WiCER CEGAR refinement

respuesta: WiCER runs a reactive CEGAR loop: it compiles a wiki, probes it with one diagnostic question per source document, and any probe scoring 1/5 is treated as a counterexample that triggers diagnosis of the dropped facts, which are then pinned as preservation constraints [2605.07068#s36.p1][2605.07068#s37.p1]. Streaming Knowledge Compilation (Online WiCER) keeps the compile–evaluate–refine structure but makes refinement proactive: because queries arrive only after each news batch, they cannot drive pinning [2606.09877#s19.p2], so a materiality signal φ_t(k,n)∈[0,1] scoring a document's importance for an entity acts as a query-relevance surrogate, letting facts be pinned before any query exposes a gap [2606.09877#s2.p3][2606.09877#s15.p1]. Concretely it mines candidate facts, scores marginal value with a state-aware scorer, pins greedily under budget B_pin with decay-weighted eviction, and compiles incrementally with periodic full recompilation [2606.09877#s2.p5]. The key conceptual shift is in what counts as a counterexample: under 'predictive CEGAR' the counterexample is a predicted high-materiality news item rather than an observed QA failure, moving refinement from diagnosis to prediction [2606.09877#s42.p1][2606.09877#s42.p4]. The prediction error ε=E[|φ_t−φ̂_t|] becomes the only domain-specific term in the regret bound O(√(T log K)) + O(B_miss·T·ε) [2606.09877#s43.p3][2606.09877#s15.p1].

pasos.argumento: Streaming Knowledge Compilation WiCER CEGAR refinement

Both find that LLM summarization at write time does not pay off relative to cheaper write strategies, though for different reasons.

3x3 study (2603.02473): write strategy matters little — accuracy spans only 3–8 points across write strategies versus 20 points across retrieval methods [2603.02473#s1.p1]. Basic RAG (zero LLM calls at write time) matches or exceeds the costlier Extracted Facts and Summarized Episodes strategies under cosine (77.9%) and hybrid (81.1%) retrieval; Summarized Episodes only wins under BM25 (62.7% vs 59.2%) [2603.02473#s8.p1]. Retrieval precision correlates with accuracy at r=0.98 [2603.02473#s9.p1].

MERIT (2609.05441): LLM summarization behaves like update-on-write and does help on hard, fact-updated tasks — C3 (LLM summary) scores 1.00/0.70/1.00 on hard, far above retrieval's 0.35–0.70, and C3−C2 is +0.44/+0.38/+0.28 across models (all p≤0.0002) [2609.05441#s22.p4][2609.05441#s29.p5]. But it is not the most cost-effective: the structured fact store C4 has the best CAMU in two of three domains, and full replay is never economical [2609.05441#s26.p1]. So summarizing at write time pays off for correctness under fact updates, but a structured update-on-write store is cheaper for the same benefit.

respuesta:
Both find that LLM summarization at write time does not pay off relative to cheaper alternatives, though for different reasons.

**3x3 study (2603.02473):** Write strategy matters little; retrieval method dominates. Accuracy spans ~20 points across retrieval methods (57.1%–77.2%) but only 3–8 points across write strategies [2603.02473#s1.p1]. Basic RAG — raw chunks with zero LLM calls at write time — matches or exceeds the costlier LLM-based strategies (Extracted Facts, Summarized Episodes) under cosine (77.9%) and hybrid (81.1%), the only exception being BM25 where Summarized Episodes edges ahead (62.7% vs 59.2%) [2603.02473#s8.p1]. So paying an LLM to summarize/extract at write time buys essentially nothing.

**MERIT (2609.05441):** LLM summarization behaves like update-on-write and does help on hard (fact-updated) tasks — C3 reaches 1.00/0.70/1.00 versus retrieval's 0.35–0.70, and C3−C2 is +0.44/+0.38/+0.28 across models [2609.05441#s22.p4][2609.05441#s29.p5]. But it is not the most cost-effective: the structured fact store C4 is best on CAMU in D1 (4,839 pts/$) and D3 (3,245), with C2 best only in D2 (6,629), and full replay never economical [2609.05441#s26.p1]. Summarization also costs more per episode than C4 or C2 ($0.00095 vs $0.00066/$0.00073) [2609.05441#s26.p1].

In short: the 3x3 study finds LLM write-time summarization adds no accuracy over raw storage; MERIT finds it does fix updated-fact failures but is dominated on cost-effectiveness by a structured update-on-write store.

respuesta: HippoRAG associates information across passages at index/retrieval time: an LLM extracts schemaless KG triples from each passage via OpenIE, retrieval encoders add synonymy edges between similar noun phrases, and query entities seed Personalized PageRank over this graph, whose node distribution is multiplied by the passage-node count matrix to score passages [2405.14831#s5.p2][2405.14831#s6.p1][2405.14831#s6.p4]. This builds an associative hippocampal-style index so multi-hop paths can be found even when relevant entities never co-occur in one passage [2405.14831#s2.p3][2405.14831#s2.p4]. TOKI, by contrast, handles contradictions at write time as concurrency control: contradicting bitemporal facts (same subject/predicate, different object, overlapping valid time) are resolved by typed operators — last-writer-wins, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy — each with an isolation precondition and admitted anomalies, returning a winner, invalidating the loser in system time, and emitting an audit tuple [2606.06240#s6.p1][2606.06240#s10.p1][2606.06240#s2.p1]. It also logs judge verdicts before commit to prevent replay inconsistency [2606.06240#s15.p2]. So HippoRAG links compatible knowledge associatively for retrieval, while TOKI adjudicates incompatible knowledge with bitemporal, isolation-indexed operators and audit records.

respuesta:
The two papers treat contradiction resolution and persistence semantics very differently. The Missing Knowledge Layer paper makes persistence semantics the organizing principle: each cognitive layer gets its own persistence mechanism, and for the Knowledge layer ("what is true") persistence is indefinite with contradiction handled by supersession — old claims are preserved and linked to successors with provenance rather than forgotten [2604.11364#s8.p1][2604.11364#s7.p3]. Memory ("what happened") instead decays (Ebbinghaus) and uses bi-temporal event sourcing [2604.11364#s9.p1], while Wisdom updates by evidence-gated revision, not supersession [2604.11364#s10.p1]. The paper argues CoALA and JEPA conflate knowledge with memory, applying identical update mechanics to facts and experiences [2604.11364#s1.p1][2604.11364#s2.p4], and cites BEAM's finding that contradiction resolution is the weakest ability (<0.05) at 10M tokens, requiring architectural rather than retrieval solutions [2604.11364#s13.p6]. Its pilot shows typed routing improving contradiction resolution from 0.394 to 0.500 [2604.11364#s20.p9].

TOKI instead frames contradiction resolution as write-time concurrency control: the four production heuristics (last-writer-wins, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy) are one family of bitemporal operators, each with an undeclared isolation precondition and admitted write-time anomalies [2606.06240#s1.p1][2606.06240#s2.p1]. Persistence semantics appear as the bitemporal fact (valid-time and system-time periods, provenance, confidence) [2606.06240#s6.p1] and the dual-row current/audit schema, where the loser is invalidated in system time and an audit tuple is emitted [2606.06240#s10.p1][2606.06240#s9.p1]. It names audit erasure (loss of the overwritten fact) as an LLM-specific anomaly N3 [2606.06240#s11.p1], which is precisely the persistence guarantee the Missing Knowledge Layer paper demands via supersession-with-provenance. So the Missing Knowledge Layer paper prescribes persistence semantics per layer and treats contradiction as supersession within the Knowledge layer, while TOKI formalizes contradiction resolution itself as a write-time contract whose correctness depends on isolation level and on retaining the overwritten fact in an audit row.

respuesta:
The Missing Knowledge Layer paper treats contradiction resolution as a property of the Knowledge layer's persistence semantics: Knowledge facts are not forgotten but superseded, with old claims preserved and linked to successors with provenance [2604.11364#s8.p1], and each layer has a distinct persistence mechanism, update rule, and scope [2604.11364#s7.p3]. It argues that conflating knowledge with memory (as in CoALA and JEPA) causes systems to apply decay to facts or identical update mechanics to facts and experiences [2604.11364#s1.p1], and it cites BEAM's near-zero contradiction resolution (<0.05) as evidence that such abilities need architectural rather than retrieval solutions [2604.11364#s13.p6]. Its pilot shows typed routing (separating Knowledge from Memory) improves contradiction resolution from 0.394 to 0.500 [2604.11364#s20.p9].

TOKI instead frames contradiction resolution as write-time concurrency control over bitemporal facts: each of the four production heuristics is a bitemporal operator with an undeclared isolation precondition and admitted anomalies [2606.06240#s1.p1][2606.06240#s2.p1]. Persistence semantics are captured by bitemporal facts (valid-time and system-time periods, provenance, confidence) [2606.06240#s6.p1] and a dual-row schema where the loser is invalidated in system time and an audit row preserves the overwritten fact [2606.06240#s10.p1][2606.06240#s9.p1]; audit erasure (N3) is the anomaly of losing that record [2606.06240#s11.p1]. Thus TOKI makes persistence (audit/bitemporal history) the precondition for correct contradiction resolution, whereas the Missing Knowledge Layer paper makes supersession-with-provenance the defining persistence semantics of the Knowledge layer.

respuesta: They differ in whether conflicting/stale information is actively removed. HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) is an indexing/retrieval framework: it builds an LLM-extracted knowledge graph (OpenIE triples plus synonym and passage nodes) and retrieves via Personalized PageRank [2405.14831#s5.p2][2502.14802#s7.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2]. It has no mechanism for handling updates or contradictions—new passages are simply added to the graph, and retrieval ranks passages by PageRank score [2405.14831#s6.p4][2502.14802#s11.p1]. GC-Mem, by contrast, is an inference-time consistency protocol aimed exactly at new/conflicting information: it formalizes Semantic Shadowing, where an updated entity's old state is not deleted and dense retrieval returns the majority of stale chunks [2609.16073#s2.p2]. GC-Mem runs a pairwise NLI conflict oracle within the retrieved candidate set and applies a temporal dominance operator that excises any older chunk contradicted by a newer one, so only the terminal state survives [2609.16073#s9.p2][2609.16073#s9.p4][2609.16073#s9.p5]. Thus HippoRAG accumulates memory without conflict resolution, while GC-Mem prunes shadowed/conflicting memories at query time (requiring a detector with >50% recall) [2609.16073#s20.p1].

They address different problems. HippoRAG (and HippoRAG 2) is an indexing/retrieval architecture: it builds an LLM-extracted knowledge graph as a hippocampal index and retrieves via Personalized PageRank, with HippoRAG 2 adding passage nodes and LLM triple filtering [2405.14831#s2.p4][2502.14802#s8.p2][2502.14802#s10.p1]. Neither page describes any mechanism for updating, superseding, or resolving conflicting memories — new passages are simply added to the graph index, and the pages report no conflict-handling protocol.

GC-Mem, by contrast, is explicitly an inference-time consistency protocol for mutable memory. It targets Semantic Shadowing: when an entity's state updates, the old state is not deleted, and dense retrieval returns the statistical majority of stale, logically contradictory chunks [2609.16073#s2.p2]. GC-Mem applies a temporal dominance operator Φ_T plus a pairwise NLI contradiction detector within the retrieved candidate set, excising any chunk contradicted by a newer one, so that if a valid chunk is retrieved all older contradictory chunks are removed [2609.16073#s9.p2][2609.16073#s9.p4]. It rejects heuristic time-decay and multi-factor scoring, which it shows protect entrenched historical errors [2609.16073#s1.p1][2609.16073#s2.p3]. Its effectiveness is bounded by detector recall rather than precision [2609.16073#s16.p3][2609.16073#s20.p1].

In short: HippoRAG handles new information by graph-based integration and associative retrieval, without an explicit conflict-resolution step; GC-Mem handles new/conflicting information by detecting contradictions and pruning temporally dominated (stale) memories at query time.
